title: Funding cuts leave northern cadets out in the cold
summary: The federal government is investing heavily in the North, but some people involved with the cadet program say Department of National Defence is short changing northern kids.

image.caption: Members of the 2837 Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry Army Cadet Corps, based in Yellowknife, demonstrate a temporary shelter. Leaders say recent federal funding cuts to the cadets could jeopardize youth activities in the North. (Submitted by Robert Gill)

blocks.text: Canada
The federal government is investing heavily in the North, but some people involved with the cadet program say Department of National Defence is short changing northern kids.
Budget constraints hit hard in North, where cadets, junior rangers may be only federally funded kids activity
Cadets and junior rangers in the North will be the worst impacted by the Canadian military halting most cadet activities due to budget constraints, cadet leaders are warning.
Recent budget constraints have restricted most cadet activities Canada-wide to weekly meetings. That means no more field training, travel or other activities.
In southern communities, it’s a blow, but there may be alternatives. In the North, it could mean the only funded activity available for kids is gone.

“The youth are losing,” said Floyd Powder. He started in the Army Cadet Corps in Fort Smith, N.W.T., when he was 12, and served in the Canadian Forces for over 30 years, including working across all three territories with the cadets and the Junior Canadian Rangers.
In a statement, Defence Minister David McGuinty said the department has “heard the concerns” about the belt-tightening measures.
But Powder isn’t sure those making the decisions have actually been listening to Northerners.

“Most decision makers that are down south don't have any or much experience in the North and they don't realize the bigger impact that this will cause,” he said. “Our youth is the biggest investment that we can make.”

Floyd Powder, left, a Métis veteran from Fort Smith, has been involved with the cadets and junior rangers for decades. At right, a photo of Powder while on a cadet exercise in Resolute Bay. (Jessica Davey-Quantick/CBC; Submitted by Floyd Powder)

In the three Arctic territories, the effect is already being felt. Robert Gill, the national executive director of the Army Cadet League of Canada, says a major set of activities that would have brought cadets to Whitehorse, Yellowknife and Iqaluit has been cancelled.
“This might be one of the only ways that a youth might be able to leave the community, meet other youth, other teenagers from across the territories, across Canada,” said Gill.
Cadet programs are offered at no cost to families, and include activities like sports, civic engagement and outdoor skills.

“Many youth and their families right now don't have the funds to support things and activities like hockey or baseball or soccer,” said Gill. “So this is one of the ways that youth can get active, families can ensure that their youth are learning valuable soft and hard skills."

It also means the on-the-land activities can’t happen. Powder is Metis and says the cadets and junior rangers are essential to making sure kids who might not otherwise have access to elders or knowledge holders get the chance to learn those skills.
“That is definitely a skill that could be lost, if it's not practiced,” said Powder.

blocks.text: The Local Support Allocation funding, used to help cover the costs associated with running the program, has also been axed. In Yellowknife, Gill says that means the Army Cadet Corps now has to find another way to pay its annual $9,000 rent bill, so they can continue their weekly meetings — the only thing left on their schedule.
Gill is optimistic that Yellowknife can come together and come up with the funds. But the smaller the population, the harder it is for a community to absorb those costs.
Earlier this week, parents received an email saying weekend training exercises and activities are paused until March as part of a move by the Department of Defence to cut back on spending. (CBC)
According to the Air Cadet League of Canada, they shouldn’t have to.

“The dedication of our volunteers and the financial contributions of cadet families cannot and must not become substitutes for adequate federal funding of the cadet program,” said president Jacquie Pepper-Journal, in a statement, stressing the long-standing commitment to barrier-free access for all, regardless of finances. “The ability of a community to raise funds should not determine the quality or accessibility of the cadet program available to its youth.”
The belt-tightening is expected to last until the end of this fiscal year, but there is no confirmation it will be loosened on April 1.
Gill said representatives from the Army, Navy and Air cadet leagues are preparing to meet with the minister before the holidays to seek clear answers.
